candidates.exact_span: 4Q3             Lowest four-day average flow rate expected to occur once every three-years
candidates.computation_change_reason: If permit limits or monitoring frequency are keyed to design or critical flow, different interpretations of the 4Q3 statistic (e.g., the averaging period, recurrence interval, or how the value is derived) could change which numeric limits apply and which monitoring obligations are triggered.

candidates.exact_span: BAT             Best available technology economically achievable
candidates.computation_change_reason: BAT is a technology-basis category for effluent limits; interpreting whether a parameter or pollutant is BAT-regulated versus governed by another standard could change which enforceable numeric limit is selected for comparison.

candidates.exact_span: BCT             Best conventional pollutant control technology
candidates.computation_change_reason: BCT defines a distinct technology-based limit framework for conventional pollutants; misclassification of a pollutant or outfall under BCT versus another basis could change the applicable numeric discharge limit.

candidates.exact_span: BPT             Best practicable control technology currently available
candidates.computation_change_reason: BPT is another technology-based limit category; different interpretations of BPT applicability could change which numeric limit governs a given parameter and discharge point.

BMP obligations may be non-numeric management or monitoring requirements distinct from effluent limits; interpreting whether a cited BMP term imposes a monitoring duty, a plan-only obligation, or no enforceable requirement could change monitoring-applicability findings and how missing numeric evidence is classified.

candidates.exact_span: BOD             Biochemical oxygen demand (five-day unless noted otherwise)
candidates.computation_change_reason: The parenthetical qualifier distinguishes five-day BOD from other BOD measurement bases; applying the wrong BOD definition could pair reported measurements with the wrong numeric limit.
Limits derived by BPJ may apply where guideline-based limits do not; interpreting whether a limit is BPJ-based affects which numeric standard is enforceable for compliance comparison.

candidates.exact_span: CBOD            Carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (five-day unless noted otherwise)
candidates.computation_change_reason: CBOD is a distinct parameter from total BOD, and the five-day qualifier matters for limit matching; conflating CBOD with BOD or another oxygen-demand measure could change the applicable numeric limit.

Critical dilution can enter water-quality-based limit calculations; different interpretations of CD values or how they are applied could change the resulting numeric discharge limit used for exceedance analysis.

What counts as a DMR affects whether submitted monitoring evidence satisfies a monitoring obligation and whether a missing ordinary numeric result should be treated as documented reporting, inadequate evidence, or another no-data state.
ELGs are a primary source of technology-based numeric limits; interpreting whether a pollutant or process is ELG-covered versus subject to another basis could change which enforceable limit applies.

ML governs how laboratory detection thresholds relate to reported values; different interpretations of ML when results are below detection or reported as less-than values could change exceedance determinations and whether evidence is treated as a valid numeric result or a missing/non-quantified state.

MQL is distinct from ML and affects whether a value is considered quantified for compliance and reporting; alternate interpretations of MQL could change limit comparisons and missing-evidence classification for borderline or non-quantified results.

Reasonable-potential findings can determine whether certain water-quality-based numeric limits are included in the permit; interpreting RP status differently could change which limits are considered applicable.
pH limits are expressed in standard units; interpreting reported pH on a different scale or unit basis could change whether a measurement exceeds the applicable numeric limit.
WLA is the allocative basis for many water-quality-based numeric limits; different interpretations of which WLA applies to a discharge could change the enforceable limit selected for comparison.

WET is a separate compliance framework with its own numeric/pass-fail criteria and testing schedule; interpreting WET requirements differently could change both applicable toxicity limits and whether specific monitoring events were required.
